blocks.text: Alcohols burn completely to carbon dioxide and water: CH3CH2OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O, delta Hc = -1367 kJ/mol. The reaction is highly exothermic, which is why ethanol is used instead of petrol in some countries.

The -OH group can be replaced by a halogen to give a halogenoalkane, e.g. CH3CH2OH + HCl -> CH3CH2Cl + H2O (ZnCl2 catalyst); the other reagents (SOCl2, PCl3, PCl5, KBr with acid) were given in topic 21.1.

A reactive metal such as sodium breaks the O-H bond of the hydroxyl group: hydrogen gas is given off and a base, an alkoxide, forms: 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na -> 2CH3CH2ONa + H2. The reaction is less vigorous than sodium with water, and less vigorous still for alcohols with longer hydrocarbon chains. It can be used as a test for an -OH group: bubbles of hydrogen show that one is present. If the excess ethanol is evaporated, white crystalline sodium ethoxide is left. With phenolphthalein present, the pink colour appears slowly with ethanol but immediately with water, showing that ethanol reacts more slowly.

blocks.text: Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols only to ketones; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised. The oxidising agents include acidified potassium dichromate(VI), K2Cr2O7, and acidified KMnO4. Dichromate is orange: when an alcohol is oxidised, orange Cr2O7 2- ions are reduced to green Cr3+ ions. Distilling the aldehyde off as it forms stops at the aldehyde; heating under reflux goes on to the carboxylic acid.

items: CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O (ethanol to ethanal), then CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH.

blocks.alt: Top: primary ethanol is oxidised to ethanal and then ethanoic acid; secondary propan-2-ol to propanone only; tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised. Bottom: three tubes of acidified dichromate after warming: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have turned green; 2-methylpropan-2-ol stays orange.
blocks.caption: Oxidation of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols and the dichromate test (original diagram after the book's equations and test tubes).
blocks.long_description: Oxidation removes the hydrogen from the -OH group and a hydrogen from the carbon carrying it. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on that carbon, so it cannot be oxidised this way. That is why only primary and secondary alcohols turn the orange dichromate solution green, which is used to tell them apart from tertiary alcohols.

blocks.title: Keep in mind
blocks.text: For potassium dichromate(VI) to act as an oxidising agent it must itself be reduced, and this reduction needs hydrogen ions (H+), which the acid provides.

blocks.title: Interesting information: the breathalyser
blocks.text: Driving after drinking alcohol is very dangerous. Traffic officers use a breathalyser to check a driver. One type oxidises the ethanol in the driver's breath; the oxidation releases electrons, and the electric current produced is proportional to the amount of alcohol.

blocks.text: Alcohols can be dehydrated to alkenes. Dehydration is a kind of elimination in which a water molecule is removed: CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O (Al2O3, heat). Other dehydrating agents are concentrated sulphuric acid and concentrated phosphoric acid.

blocks.alt: Four boxes around CH3CH2OH: combustion, C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O, delta H = -1367 kJ/mol; substitution, C2H5OH + HCl -> C2H5Cl + H2O with ZnCl2; with sodium, 2C2H5OH + 2Na -> 2C2H5ONa + H2; dehydration, C2H5OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O over hot Al2O3 or with concentrated acids.
blocks.caption: Combustion, substitution, the reaction with sodium and dehydration of ethanol (original summary of the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: Combustion breaks the whole molecule; substitution replaces the -OH group; sodium replaces only the hydrogen of the -OH group; dehydration removes H2O to leave a C=C double bond.
